questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A falling birth rate and the dividend
questions.learningObjective: Identify the mechanism by which a falling birth rate can benefit a society
questions.stem: Your civic brief notes that a city's births fell steadily for two decades while its working-age population kept growing. Why can this produce a demographic dividend?

options.text: Fewer dependants per worker means more of the nation's income can be saved or invested
A smaller child population automatically raises the productivity of every adult worker
options.misconception: treats a dependency ratio as a productivity measure

options.text: Lower birth rates mean the city can spend less on schools and more on new housing
options.misconception: assumes freed spending becomes productive investment

options.text: Fewer children per family raise the average wage without any change in output
options.misconception: assumes wages rise when output does not

questions.explanation: A falling birth rate lowers the number of dependants per worker, so a larger share of income is available for saving, investment and consumption. It does not by itself raise productivity or wages, and freed spending does not become investment.
questions.hint: Ask what the dependency ratio does to saving.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Ageing and the public budget
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an ageing population changes public spending
questions.stem: Draft a paragraph for a council budget on how a rising share of old people changes what a council must spend on.

answer.exemplar: A good answer explains that as the old share of the population rises, the number of pensioners and people needing health and care grows relative to the number of workers paying in, so the spending per worker rises even where services to the young are unchanged. It notes that the pressure falls on the tax base and on borrowing, and that this is a slow, predictable trend rather than a sudden shock.

questions.explanation: More dependants per worker means higher spending per taxpayer, which the council must meet from a smaller working base. A good answer links the age structure to the bill per worker rather than to absolute totals.
questions.hint: Express it as cost per worker, not total cost.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Conditions that make a dividend usable
questions.learningObjective: Read a dependency table for the arithmetic of a dividend

stimulus.body: A district table shows the population in three groups in 1881 and in 1901. In 1881 there were 41,000 under 15, 54,000 aged 15 to 64 and 5,000 over 64. In 1901 there were 39,000 under 15, 79,000 aged 15 to 64 and 9,000 over 64. A note records that 68 percent of the district's adults were in employment in 1901.

questions.stem: Your pension fund note records the table above. What does it show about the district's demographic position?

options.text: That the number of children fell enough to shrink the working population as well
options.misconception: confuses a fall in one group with a fall in another

options.text: That the district was already ageing, because the over-64 group grew by 80 percent
options.misconception: calls a small group with a large percentage change an aged society

options.text: That fewer dependants per worker and high employment together create room for saving
That the district's population shrank, because only 127,000 people are counted
options.misconception: infers a shrinking population from a single year's total

questions.explanation: In 1901 there were 48,000 dependants against 79,000 workers, compared with 46,000 against 54,000 in 1881, so dependants per worker fell sharply while 68 percent of adults worked. That combination is what turns a demographic shift into usable savings.
questions.hint: Compute dependants per worker in both years.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the telegraph changed
questions.learningObjective: Identify the central change the telegraph made to commercial information

stimulus.body: An exchange report records that before the telegraph, a merchant in one city might act on a commodity price weeks after it had changed in the producing region. The report notes that with the telegraph the same price could be acted on within the hour, and that the change arrived in a printed column.

questions.stem: Your studio brief cites the exchange report above. What is the central change the report records?

options.text: That the telegraph ended the trading of commodities in the producing regions
options.misconception: claims a new technology removed the trade it sped up

options.text: That commodity prices rose because traders could act on them faster
options.misconception: infers a price level effect from a speed effect

options.text: That printed price columns were replaced by the telegraph as the only source
options.misconception: invents a replacement the report does not describe

options.text: That the delay between a price change and a trader's response collapsed from weeks to hours

questions.explanation: The report's measure is the gap between a price change in the producing region and a trader's ability to respond, and the telegraph compressed that gap from weeks to hours. It does not end trading, push prices up, or remove the printed column.
questions.hint: Ask what interval the technology shortened.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A price learned hours earlier
questions.learningObjective: Assess what faster price information does to a trading market
questions.stem: Your site brief compares two mill towns where one received commodity news by telegraph and the other by steamer. Draft the assessment.

options.text: The telegraph town could buy cheaper before rivals knew, but its advantage narrowed as others connected
The telegraph town was permanently richer, since the news advantage could not be copied
options.misconception: treats a copying technology as a permanent edge

options.text: The steamer town was safer, because slower news meant it never gambled on prices
options.misconception: reads slower information as prudence

options.text: Neither town was affected, since commodity prices were set in a single exchange hall
options.misconception: assumes a single price setting place for all markets

questions.explanation: Earlier information let a trader act before rivals could, but the advantage shrank as more participants joined the telegraph, so it produced a period of superior margins rather than permanent wealth. Slower news was not prudence, and prices were not set in one hall.
questions.hint: Ask what happens when others subscribe too.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Where electricity put the factory
questions.learningObjective: Explain how electric power changed where factories could be built
questions.stem: Your transport study compares a factory that moved from a riverside mill to an inland site once electric power arrived. What was the decisive change?

options.text: The inland site had a lower wage bill because the countryside was cheaper to live in
options.misconception: credits a real but secondary factor as the decisive one

options.text: Power now reached the site, so the need for a nearby river or coalfield disappeared
The inland site could borrow more money, because lenders preferred new buildings
options.misconception: invents a credit effect that powered mills did not need

options.text: The riverside mill was closed by law once electricity became widely available
options.misconception: invents a legal closure

questions.explanation: Steam power tied a factory to coal and water at its site, while electric power let a plant be placed by labour, transport and land costs instead. That release from the fuel constraint is what moved mills away from the rivers.
questions.hint: Ask what the old location was actually needed for.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A report on firms that moved
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a report on relocating firms reveals about industrial change
questions.stem: Write a short analysis for a planning committee on what a report of firms moving into and out of a district shows.

answer.exemplar: A good answer explains that a relocation report counts firm movements rather than output or employment, and that the pattern of who moves reveals which new advantages have drawn investment, such as power, transport links or available sites. It adds that the firms which leave are often the ones whose technology or location has been overtaken, so the report shows industrial restructuring rather than a simple decline.

questions.explanation: A relocation report shows where new advantage has drawn firms and which old locations have been overtaken. A good answer notes that firm counts are a proxy, not a measure of output.
questions.hint: Ask what the report does not measure.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a tabulating machine did to a census office
questions.learningObjective: Read a census office note for the work a tabulator took over

stimulus.body: A census office note records that the enumerators' returns for the national count arrived on 8,100 separate cards, that clerks had previously sorted such returns by hand, and that the office now read each card onto a machine that counted and grouped the totals, and that the first complete tabulation took six days against an estimated forty for hand work.

questions.stem: Your archive note records the census office note above. What does it show?

options.text: That the machine moved the counting and grouping work from clerks to machinery
That the machine collected the answers from households without enumerators
options.misconception: claims the machine did the fieldwork

options.text: That hand sorting had been impossible before, so the office had no other method
options.misconception: invents a lack of any earlier method

options.text: That the count became six days long in total, from enumeration to printed table
options.misconception: confuses tabulation time with the whole census

questions.explanation: The note contrasts forty days of hand sorting with six days of machine tabulation, so the machine took over counting and grouping while enumeration was untouched. It did not collect answers at all.
questions.hint: Ask which task the machine took over.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A falling birth rate and the dividend
questions.learningObjective: Read a civic note for the pattern of a demographic dividend

stimulus.body: A civic note records that between 1870 and 1900 the city's births fell from 7,400 to 4,900 a year, that the number of residents aged 20 to 40 rose by 40 percent, and that the council's income per head rose by 26 percent over the same period.

questions.stem: Your housing brief projects the working population of a city over thirty years. What does the note suggest?

options.text: That income per head fell, because more adults means fewer goods for each person
options.misconception: reverses the relationship between adult numbers and output

options.text: That more working adults with fewer dependants coincided with rising income per head
That the falling birth rate alone caused the rise in income per head
options.misconception: attributes the whole change to one factor

options.text: That the city would soon face a labour shortage as births kept falling
options.misconception: reads a rising working population as an imminent shortage

questions.explanation: Fewer dependants per worker and a growing working population coincided with a 26 percent rise in income per head, which is the pattern of a demographic dividend. The note records coincidence rather than sole cause, and the city was not short of workers.
questions.hint: Look at the ratio, not the raw birth count.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Ageing and the public budget
questions.learningObjective: Weigh two responses to an ageing population's budget pressure
questions.stem: Your municipal budget annex shows pension and health spending rising as the workforce shrinks. Draft an assessment of the options.

options.text: Cut pension benefits immediately, because the cost is the only thing that matters
options.misconception: recommends an instant cut with no regard to contracts

options.text: Raise the retirement age at once, because age alone determines who works
options.misconception: treats age as the only factor in labour supply

options.text: Raise the workforce share through participation and later retirement, alongside slower cost growth
Do nothing, because age structures always correct themselves without policy
options.misconception: assumes demographics self-correct without delay

questions.explanation: Broadening participation and adjusting retirement lengthens the working share without cutting promised benefits, and slower growth in health costs eases the same pressure. Immediate benefit cuts and instant retirement-age changes ignore contracts and the many factors behind labour supply.
questions.hint: Look for the option that widens the base without cutting promises.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Conditions that make a dividend usable
questions.learningObjective: Identify the conditions that make a demographic dividend usable
questions.stem: Your design brief asks why a falling birth rate does not automatically produce a demographic dividend. Which condition is decisive?

options.text: The government must tax the working population heavily to build a savings fund
options.misconception: assumes heavy taxation is the decisive step

options.text: The dividend must be paid out as cash to families with few children
options.misconception: confuses a social payment with the mechanism itself

options.text: The workforce must leave the region once it has been made larger
options.misconception: invents out-migration as a condition of the dividend

options.text: The extra earners must find work, and the savings must be invested rather than spent

questions.explanation: A dividend exists only as potential: without jobs the extra workers are unemployed, and without saving and investment the freed resources are consumed. Neither heavy taxation nor out-migration is the decisive step.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the extra workers and the extra saving.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the telegraph changed
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the telegraph changed the speed and reach of commercial information
questions.stem: Prepare a brief for a heritage panel on how the telegraph changed the speed and reach of commercial information.

answer.exemplar: A good answer explains that before the telegraph, news of a harvest, a strike or a price travelled by ship or coach and arrived weeks late, so decisions were made on stale information. It adds that the telegraph reduced the delay to hours and reached towns without a port, which compressed the time in which a price advantage could be exploited and shifted trading toward cities where the wires converged.

questions.explanation: The telegraph cut the lag between an event and traders hearing of it from weeks to hours, and reached inland towns too. A good answer links that speed to the window for profitable action.
questions.hint: Ask what the delay had been before.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A price learned hours earlier
questions.learningObjective: Read a broker's ledger for the value of hours-earlier information

stimulus.body: A broker's ledger for a commodity records purchases made on the strength of price news received by telegraph on the morning of the third, and on the same day the local price rose by a quarter between the morning and the close. A note adds that the previous year's purchases had been made only after a week's delay in receiving the same information.

questions.stem: Your financial history seminar cites the broker's ledger above. What does the ledger show?

options.text: That hours of earlier information let the broker buy before the local price rose
That the local price rose because the broker's purchases caused the increase
options.misconception: reverses cause and effect between buying and price

options.text: That the telegraph made the commodity price rise by a quarter each week
options.misconception: treats the price change as the technology's effect

options.text: That the week's delay had no effect, because prices moved anyway over time
options.misconception: assumes the delay never mattered

questions.explanation: The ledger pairs hours-old information with purchases made before the price rose, which is the mechanism of a trading advantage. It does not show the purchases causing the rise, nor that the technology raised prices, nor that the old delay was harmless.
questions.hint: Ask what the broker knew and when.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Where electricity put the factory
questions.learningObjective: Read a power company ledger for the release of factory location

stimulus.body: A power company's ledger lists connections made in 1898 at 24 sites, most of them new mills in a town two miles from the river. A note records that the mills had formerly stood beside the water and that the company supplied them with power at a fixed annual charge.

questions.stem: Your industrial design brief cites the power company's ledger above. What does it indicate?

options.text: The mills moved because the riverbanks had become too expensive for them
options.misconception: invents a land price motive the ledger does not give

options.text: Electric supply released the mills from the riverside and let them choose sites freely
The company bought the mills and moved them itself to collect the charges
options.misconception: attributes relocation to the supplier rather than the firms

options.text: The fixed charge was so high that the mills closed rather than move
options.misconception: invents a closure the ledger contradicts

questions.explanation: The mills previously stood beside the water and now stand two miles away, which is what a supply independent of the watercourse makes possible. The ledger shows no purchase by the company and no closure.
questions.hint: Compare the old site with the new one.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A report on firms that moved
questions.learningObjective: Assess the effects of industrial relocation on a town
questions.stem: Your planning submission asks you to assess a town that has gained one large works and lost eleven small ones. Draft the assessment.

options.text: The town has declined, since losing eleven firms always outweighs gaining one
options.misconception: counts firms instead of weighing their size

options.text: The town has grown, because one new works is always bigger than several old ones
options.misconception: assumes size from the count of firms

options.text: The outcome turns on employment, wages and local supply, not on the number of firms
The town should refuse all new firms, since arrivals always precede local closures
options.misconception: treats correlation of arrivals and closures as causation

questions.stem: Your museum interpretation panel explains the effect of a tabulating machine. Which change did it make most possible?

options.text: It allowed the census to ask each person many more questions
options.misconception: confuses faster processing with a wider questionnaire

options.text: It removed the need for enumerators to visit households in person
options.misconception: claims the machine replaced the fieldwork

options.text: It allowed the official figures to be revised without re-collecting data
options.misconception: invents a revision route that still needs new cards

options.text: It allowed officials to publish cross-tabulations that clerks could not produce

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A falling birth rate and the dividend
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a falling birth rate changes a society's spending priorities
questions.stem: Write an explanation for a council on how a falling birth rate changes what a society has to spend money on.

answer.exemplar: A good answer explains that fewer children mean less pressure on schools, clinics and housing for families, while the working population grows in relative size, so the share of public money spent on the young shrinks without anyone choosing to cut it. It adds that this creates room to spend on infrastructure, skill or saving, and that the shift is slow and often unnoticed because each budget still looks the same.

questions.explanation: Fewer children reduce the call on schools and family services while the working share grows, which frees resources without anyone cutting a programme. A good answer notes the change is gradual and easily missed.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the school budget.

questions.topic: Ageing and the public budget
questions.learningObjective: Read a council account for the fiscal pressure of ageing

stimulus.body: A council account compares two decades. In the first, spending on pensions, infirmaries and home help was 18 percent of the total budget; in the second it was 31 percent, while spending on schools fell from 24 to 19 percent of the budget, and the number of ratepayers rose by only 4 percent.

questions.stem: Your council finance note records the account above. What does it show?

options.text: That the cost of the old has risen faster than the number of those paying
That the council chose to spend more on the old rather than on schools
options.misconception: reads a share shift as a deliberate reallocation

options.text: That fewer children caused the school budget to fall by five percentage points
options.misconception: attributes a budget share to the birth rate alone

options.text: That ratepayers' numbers have nothing to do with the pressure on the budget
options.misconception: dismisses the tax base as irrelevant

questions.explanation: Spending on the old rose from 18 to 31 percent of the budget while ratepayers grew only 4 percent, so cost grew faster than the base paying for it. The school share fell with fewer children, not by choice.
questions.hint: Compare the two percentages with the ratepayer growth.

questions.topic: Conditions that make a dividend usable
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a demographic dividend's possibility from its realisation

stimulus.body: A village survey found that over twenty years the number of births per thousand fell from 38 to 29, that the number of residents of working age rose by 30 percent, that a factory that opened nearby took most of the new workers, and that almost none of the extra earnings were put into savings or local businesses.

questions.stem: Your market analysis note records the village survey above. What does it show?

options.text: The village captured the demographic dividend in full, because the age structure improved
options.misconception: counts the arithmetic as if the outcome had been realised

options.text: The age structure improved, but the extra earnings were consumed rather than invested
The factory failed, because a falling birth rate reduced the local labour supply
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the labour effect

options.text: The village could have saved more, because its workers were unusually well paid
options.misconception: invents a wage level the survey never gives

questions.explanation: The demographic arithmetic improved and the extra workers found work in the new factory, but nothing was saved or invested, so the potential surplus was consumed. A good answer separates the possibility of a dividend from its realisation.

questions.topic: What the telegraph changed
questions.learningObjective: Judge how the telegraph affected the advantage of an early user
questions.stem: Your heritage brief asks you to judge how the telegraph affected the first users of a line compared with later ones. Draft the assessment.

options.text: Early users gained most, because the line was shortest and cheapest for them
options.misconception: confuses physical length with informational advantage

options.text: Early users gained nothing, since the service only worked once many towns connected
options.misconception: assumes no network effect in the early years

options.text: Early users earned an advantage that narrowed as more towns and firms joined the network
Later users gained most, because the equipment was newer and more reliable
options.misconception: credits equipment quality for the later advantage

questions.topic: A price learned hours earlier
questions.learningObjective: Identify the effect of receiving price news hours earlier
questions.stem: A merchant in one port hears a commodity price change hours before merchants in an inland town. What advantage does the first merchant hold?

options.text: A guaranteed higher margin, because the early price cannot be wrong
options.misconception: treats faster news as certainty

options.text: A permanent price advantage, since the inland towns can never catch up
options.misconception: assumes information gaps cannot close

options.text: Lower risk, because early news removes the need to hedge a position
options.misconception: claims early news removes market risk

options.text: A time advantage in acting, while it lasts before the news spreads

questions.stem: Set out for a district plan how electric power changed where industry could locate itself.

answer.exemplar: A good answer explains that steam power obliged a factory to stand where coal was cheap or where falling water was available, which fixed many mills on rivers and in coalfield valleys. questions.explanation: Steam tied industry to fuel and water, and electricity freed it to choose by labour, transport and land. A good answer names the old constraint and the new pattern.

questions.learningObjective: Assess what a council should do with resources freed by a falling birth rate
questions.stem: Your council briefing asks how it should use the resources freed as school-age numbers fall. Draft the assessment.

options.text: Spend them on new school buildings, since the buildings will outlast the children
options.misconception: commits capital to a declining demand

options.text: Cut them from the budget, since the savings will not be needed again
options.misconception: assumes the freed money will never be wanted later

options.text: Invest them in skills, infrastructure or a savings fund, so the surplus becomes capital
Spend them on pensions, since the old will soon need more care
options.misconception: assumes an immediate and certain elderly pressure

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Ageing and the public budget
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an ageing population's budget effect from its growth effect
questions.stem: Your finance committee brief asks what an ageing population does to a budget as distinct from what it does to economic growth. Which statement is right?

options.text: It lowers the budget, because older residents claim less public spending
options.misconception: reverses the direction of spending on the old

options.text: It slows growth, because older workers are always less productive
options.misconception: attributes a productivity judgement to age alone

options.text: It raises spending per worker, and it can slow growth, but the two are separate
It affects only growth, and the tax base rises to pay for it automatically

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Conditions that make a dividend usable
questions.learningObjective: Explain the conditions under which a demographic dividend is realised
questions.stem: Explain to a planning committee what must happen for a demographic dividend to be realised rather than merely possible.

answer.exemplar: A good answer explains that the dividend is an arithmetic possibility: more earners and fewer dependants. It then sets out the conditions, namely enough employment in productive work, an education that raises the earning capacity of those workers, savings that are actually invested, and institutions that let the working generation keep more of what it earns. It notes that without each of these the surplus is consumed or lost.

questions.explanation: The dividend is a possibility created by the age structure, and it becomes real only if there is work, skill, saving and investment. A good answer names each condition and says what happens when it is missing.
questions.hint: Ask what turns the possibility into a result.

That steamer mail was slower before the telegraph than it was afterwards

options.misconception: claims a wholesale replacement the note does not describe

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A price learned hours earlier
questions.learningObjective: Explain how faster price information redistributed gain between traders
questions.stem: Summarise for a merchant's guild how learning a price hours earlier changed where gains went.

answer.exemplar: A good answer explains that when news of a price change reaches traders at different moments, the earliest informed buyers and sellers capture the difference between the old and the new price, and the last to act may trade at the new price without any advantage. It adds that as the information network spread, the earlier traders' edge narrowed and the gain moved towards those with the fastest and most reliable wires rather than towards those with the most capital.

questions.explanation: The gain from a price change accrues to whoever acts first on the news and disappears for whoever acts last. A good answer shows how that window shrinks as the information network spreads.
questions.hint: Ask who trades at the old price and who at the new one.

options.text: The dividend ends as those large working cohorts themselves reach old age

questions.stem: Argue for a finance committee why an ageing population is harder for a budget to adjust to than most trends.

answer.exemplar: A good answer explains that the pressure arrives gradually over decades, so no single year looks like a crisis and each budget can defer the problem a little. It notes that the costs are largely committed in advance by pension rules and long-term care contracts, that the working population shrinks at the same time, and that the adjustment therefore has to be made early and in small steps or suddenly and painfully.

questions.explanation: Ageing pressure builds slowly, so budgets can defer it, yet pension and care commitments are locked in while the base shrinks. A good answer links the slowness to the difficulty of adjusting in time.
questions.hint: Ask how quickly the pressure appears.

questions.topic: What the telegraph changed
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the telegraph changed where trade concentrated
questions.stem: Account for a traders' society why the telegraph changed where trade concentrated.

answer.exemplar: A good answer explains that before the lines, information moved with goods and ships, so trading concentrated at ports that already handled the cargo and could not act on news from further inland. It adds that the telegraph carried prices towards inland centres that could now buy before the goods arrived, which drew middlemen, brokers and insurers inland and shifted the geography of commercial cities towards wherever the wires converged.

questions.explanation: Information used to travel with goods, so trade clustered at ports; the wires carried prices inland and drew brokers and insurers after them. A good answer links the change in information to the change in commercial geography.
questions.hint: Ask where information now travelled separately from cargo.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A price learned hours earlier
questions.learningObjective: Read an insurance note for the effect of faster quotes

stimulus.body: An insurance note records that before the telegraph, a shipper insured cargo for a voyage of several weeks at rates quoted in the home market, and that after the wires were connected the same shipper could insure in the port against a quote obtained the same morning, with a shorter exposure to price movement.

questions.stem: Your exchange floor briefing cites the insurance note above. What does the note show?

options.text: That faster information shortened the period in which a price could move against a trader
That insurance premiums fell because fewer ships sank after the wires were laid
options.misconception: invents a shipping safety effect

options.text: That the telegraph set insurance rates directly, replacing the market's quotes
options.misconception: claims the technology replaced the quoting market

options.text: That shippers no longer needed cover, because voyages had become shorter
options.misconception: misreads a change in exposure as a change in need

questions.explanation: Insurance let a shipper fix a price over weeks of exposure, whereas a quote obtained the same morning cut that exposure to hours. Nothing in the note concerns shipwrecks, rate-setting or a shorter voyage.
questions.hint: Ask what period the shipper was exposed to.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Where electricity put the factory
questions.learningObjective: Read a grid notice for the generalisation of power supply

stimulus.body: A grid extension notice states that supply would be extended for six miles from the generating station at a fixed annual charge, that the extension would serve any works choosing to connect, and that several mills which had refused an earlier private supply had now applied for connection.

questions.stem: Your regional survey records that several mills applied for connection. What does the notice show?

options.text: That power was becoming a service available on general terms rather than a private bargain
That the mills had grown, since they could now afford a power supply
options.misconception: assumes growth from a connection application

options.text: That the earlier private supply had been cheaper than the grid rate
options.misconception: invents a price comparison the notice does not give

options.text: That the mills had refused power for reasons of principle
options.misconception: invents a motive the notice does not record

questions.explanation: An extension offered to any works at a fixed charge replaces the earlier situation in which power came from a private arrangement, which is what moved several reluctant mills to apply. Nothing in the notice shows growth, a price comparison or a principled refusal.
questions.hint: Ask what changed in the terms of supply.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A report on firms that moved
questions.learningObjective: Weigh two policies for attracting firms to a district
questions.stem: Your industrial policy brief asks you to weigh a rates holiday against building a works training school. Draft the assessment.

options.text: The rates holiday is better, because rates are the only cost a firm bears
options.misconception: reduces a firm's costs to a single item

options.text: The training school is better, because firms never need trained labour locally
options.misconception: ignores the local labour requirement

options.text: The holiday helps a firm that has decided to stay, while the school supplies the workers it needs
Both are wasteful, because firms should simply be left to choose their locations
options.misconception: assumes location decisions need no public preparation

questions.explanation: A rates holiday lowers the cost of a decision already taken, which is useful for a firm at the margin but does little for a district without the labour or suppliers the industry requires. A training school builds that capacity, so the two act on different sides of the decision.
questions.hint: Ask at which stage of the decision each helps.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a tabulating machine did to a census office
questions.learningObjective: Identify the work a tabulating machine did not replace
questions.stem: Your museum label asks which part of census work a tabulating machine did not replace. What is it?

options.text: The sorting of returns into groups, which the machine took over completely
options.misconception: names work the machine actually did

options.text: The transcription of the enumerators' answers onto cards for reading
options.misconception: names the step the machine performed

options.text: The checking of cards before they were read by the machine
options.misconception: names the task that remained with clerks

options.text: The visiting of households by enumerators to gather the answers

questions.explanation: Enumerators still had to visit households and transcribe what they were told; the machine began only at the point of reading the cards and counting them. Checking cards also stayed with clerks, which is why their work changed rather than disappeared.
questions.hint: Ask which step came first in the chain.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A falling birth rate and the dividend
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a falling birth rate changes a population's dependency structure
questions.stem: Show a demographic conference how a falling birth rate changes the dependency structure of a population.

answer.exemplar: A good answer explains that the child share falls first, so the ratio of dependants to working adults drops and the total dependency burden may even fall while the absolute number of old people rises. It notes that this state is temporary, because the smaller cohorts will themselves age into old age and the burden then returns at a higher level, which is why the opportunity has a time limit built into it.

questions.explanation: A falling child share lowers the dependency ratio before the old-age share rises, so the burden can fall even as the old population grows. A good answer notes that the state is temporary by arithmetic.
questions.hint: Ask which age group falls first.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Ageing and the public budget
questions.learningObjective: Read a works benefit record for the cost of an ageing scheme

stimulus.body: A works benefit record for a district lists 1,900 pensioners in 1881 and 4,600 in 1901, records that the standard pension age had been lowered from 65 to 60 in 1890, and shows expenditure on the scheme rising from 92,000 to 310,000 pounds while the district's adult population rose from 31,000 to 39,000.

questions.stem: Your pension brief asks who bears the cost of the scheme. What does the record show?

options.text: That spending per adult rose sharply, made worse by a lower pension age
That the scheme was failing, since spending per adult more than doubled
options.misconception: reads a rising per head cost as insolvency

options.text: That the rise in pensioners was caused entirely by the lower pension age
options.misconception: attributes the whole increase to one policy change

options.text: That the district's adults grew enough to absorb the extra cost with ease
options.misconception: ignores the change in cost per adult

questions.explanation: Expenditure per adult rose from about 3 pounds to about 8 pounds while the adult population grew by a quarter, and the lowered pension age added claimants who would otherwise have kept working. A higher per head cost is a political burden, not a solvency failure.
questions.hint: Compare spending with the adult population.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Conditions that make a dividend usable
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a demographic window can pass without being used

stimulus.body: A district record shows that over a decade the share of adults in paid employment fell from 78 percent to 61 percent even as the number of adults rose sharply, that most of the new adults were women who had not worked before, and that a local textile works had closed during the period.

questions.stem: Your regional report on moving firms lists a closure in the district. What does the record suggest?

options.text: The demographic window was real but not used, because work and training were missing
The window was never real, because the birth rate fall was too small to matter
options.misconception: dismisses the arithmetic without reading the employment figures

options.text: The textile closure was caused by the district's falling birth rate
options.misconception: invents a demographic cause for an industrial closure

options.text: The women were excluded from work by law, so no amount of training would help
options.misconception: invents a legal exclusion the record does not state

questions.explanation: The extra adults existed but the share in paid employment fell sharply, with much of the new working population previously inactive, so the window passed without becoming output or saving. The closure is context, not cause.
questions.hint: Ask whether the extra earners actually worked.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the telegraph changed
questions.learningObjective: Assess the effect of the telegraph on the pace of commercial decisions
questions.stem: Your business history seminar asks you to assess the effect of the telegraph on how quickly commercial decisions were made. Draft the assessment.

options.text: Decisions became quick and uniform, because everyone acted on the same information at once
options.misconception: assumes simultaneous and identical decisions

options.text: Decisions became quick for those with the wires and slow for everyone else
options.misconception: assumes a permanent two tier market

options.text: Decisions accelerated and were taken on fresher information, which rewarded readiness to act
Decisions barely changed, because merchants had always acted on the latest news they had
options.misconception: ignores the change in what the latest news meant

questions.explanation: The telegraph made information arrive within hours, so decisions were taken on fresher facts and a trader ready to move could act before rivals had read the same wire. Speed rewarded preparedness rather than producing identical decisions for everyone.
questions.hint: Ask who gained from moving quickly.
